earlier_scan.source_named: Checked Constenla Umana 1987 'Elementos de fonologia comparada de las lenguas misumalpas' (read online): reconstruction of suprasegmentals explicitly excluded; no Matagalpa stress statement.

new_statements.quote: Una buena parte de los vocablos terminan en vocales acentuadas, como Tomabú, Senisabú, Bumbulé, Gualasá, Jamailí, Yucumbé, Alabatú, Paclí, Tumbé, Tapacusí, etc. En algunos vocablos hay cambios de acentuación sustituyendo la í acentuada y tornando grave el vocablo: Cuslí o Cusile, Chuslí o Chusle, Salalí o Salale, Yarají o Yaraje, Apanasí o Apanaje, Soní o Sonis, etc.
new_statements.translation: A good part of the words end in accented vowels, e.g. Tomabú, Senisabú, Bumbulé, Gualasá, Jamailí, Yucumbé, Alabatú, Paclí, Tumbé, Tapacusí, etc. In some words there are changes of accentuation, the accented í being replaced and the word becoming paroxytone: Cuslí or Cusile, Chuslí or Chusle, Salalí or Salale, Yarají or Yaraje, Apanasí or Apanaje, Soní or Sonis, etc.
new_statements.citation: Incer [Barquero], Jaime. 1985. Toponimias indígenas de Nicaragua. San José, C.R.: Libro Libre. 481 pp. (chapter 'Los Matagalpas', pp. 263-288); same passage earlier in Incer, Jaime. 1984. "Nombres geográficos derivados de la lengua matagalpa y de voces aborígenes afines." Revista del Pensamiento Centroamericano 183: 55-84, at p. 57.
new_statements.locator: 1985 book p. 272 (p. 270), chapter 'Los Matagalpas', just before 'Investigaciones previas'; = 1984 article p. 57
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: other-problem. Incer's remark concerns the accentuation of Matagalpa-derived place names and faunal loans as pronounced in Nicaraguan Spanish (oxytone -lí, -bú, -sí endings, some hispanised to paroxytone), written a century after the language went extinct; it is not a statement about Matagalpa word stress - keep at most as a pointer. | checker: lines 368-373 (printed p. 272, just before 'Investigaciones previas') carries the passage; scanned renders 'Jamailí' as 'Ja-madi' and 'Salalí o Salale' as 'alío Salale', otherwise identical; the 1984 RPC 183 version ( lines 3302-3308, p. 57) matches A's wording except scanned 'Alabará'/'Paraje'. I read the surrounding chapter: it is…
new_statements.relation_note: Incidental observation in a toponymic gazetteer: a good part of the Matagalpa-derived words (place names) end in an accented (stressed) vowel, with some doublets where the stressed final -i is replaced and the word becomes paroxytone (Cusli ~ Cusile). Not a description of the language's word stress; based on place names as pronounced in Nicaraguan Spanish.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tendency statement only: many Matagalpa toponyms/loanwords are oxytone (final stressed vowel, esp. the endings -lí, -bú, -bé, -sá, -sí); some alternate with paroxytone Spanish-adapted forms. No rule for the language's lexicon is given.
new_statements.exceptions: doublets Cuslí~Cusile, Chuslí~Chusle, Salalí~Salale, Yarají~Yaraje, Apanasí~Apanaje, Soní~Sonis (final stress lost, word becomes 'grave')
new_statements.identity_note: Toponymic study of place names of the central-northwest highlands (Nueva Segovia, Madriz, Esteli, Matagalpa, W Jinotega) attributed to the Matagalpa language (mata1288); the material is hispanicized toponyms and loanwords, not recorded Matagalpa speech. The 1984 article version (RPC 183) is already held by the project as but is not in our bibliography.

sources.citation: Bertoglia Richards, Mafalda. 1988. La lengua cacaopera: fonología y léxico. Tesis de maestría, Universidad de Costa Rica.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Full phonology of Cacaopera (caca1244), Matagalpa's closest sister; if the catalog accepts a sister-language proxy or wants Cacaopera itself, this is the likeliest place for a stress statement in the Matagalpan branch.
sources.venue: Tesis de maestría, Universidad de Costa Rica

sources.citation: Pache, Matthias. 2024. "Tracing sound change in Nasa Yuwe: Evidence from Andaqui and Misumalpan languages." LIAMES: Linguas Indigenas Americanas 24: 1-44. DOI 10.20396/liames.v24i00.8673031
sources.note: Phonological content is segmental only: Proto-Misumalpan vowel and consonant inventories after Constenla 1987 (Tables 9-10), reflexes in daughter languages, lexical comparison sets; Matagalpa appears as isolated cited forms with Lehmann's diacritics reproduced but never discussed. a full-text search for stress/accent/prosod/syllable: no hits. Nothing on word stress or tone for Matagalpa or any Matagalpan language.

sources.citation: Kuhl Arauz, Eddy. 2015 (11 February). "Busqueda centenaria de 'Matagalpa-parlantes'." Mosaico CSI (blog of a Matagalpa cultural centre), online.
sources.note: No phonology. The single 'acento' hit is an author's note on the ethnonym as pronounced in Nicaraguan Spanish (Ulu'a vs U'lua/Ulwa); not a statement about Matagalpa word stress.

sources.citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo. 2011. "Estado de conservación y documentación de las lenguas de America Central pertenecientes a las agrupaciones jicaque, lenca, misumalpa, chibchense y chocó." Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 37(1): 135-195. DOI 10.15517/rfl.v37i1.2353.
sources.note: No phonology content for Matagalpa; states authoritatively that the only data are 7 short word lists in Lehmann (1920: 599-604) and, in the sec. 3.1.6 table (p. 150), that Matagalpa data = 'vocabulario', source = 'observadores', analysed/ordered = 'no', product = none (contrast Cacaopera: 'sistema fonematico'). I.e. no phonemic or prosodic analysis of Matagalpa has ever been produced.
sources.venue: Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica

sources.citation: Kuhl Arauz, Eddy. 2011 (8 March). "Vocabulario del lenguaje 'matagalpa' (Nicaragua)." Revista Vinculando (online). [web version of the author's Matagalpa vocabulary compilation, cf. Kuhl 2008 RTN 8 and Kuhl 2018 RTN 120 already held]
sources.note: History of the documentation plus Spanish-Matagalpa word list; a full-text search for stress/accent acento/acentuacion/aguda/tonica/pronunciacion/silaba over the page text: no remark on accent or stress; accent marks on some items are copied from the sources without comment (wordlist-only data, not a statement).

sources.citation: Kuhl [Kühl Arauz], Eddy. 2008. "Indios matagalpas y su lengua ¿quiénes eran?" Revista de Temas Nicaragüenses 8 (diciembre 2008): 31-36.
sources.note: No phonology content; only notes that Lehmann's list uses 'ortografía española, y fonética alemana'. Word lists reprinted without discussion of accent.

sources.citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo. 2002. "Acerca de la relación genealógica de las lenguas lencas y las lenguas misumalpas." Revista de Filología y Lingüística 28(1): 189-205. DOI 10.15517/rfl.v28i1.4509
sources.note: Lexical/genealogical comparison only; Matagalpa excluded from the glottochronological count because 'el léxico disponible es excesivamente exiguo'. Nothing on stress. Bibliography names Moreira González 1986 (licenciatura thesis, lexicostatistics incl. Matagalpa) and Bertoglia Richards 1988 (MA thesis, Cacaopera phonology).

sources.citation: Van Broekhoven, Laura N. K. 2002. Conquistando lo invencible: fuentes históricas sobre las culturas indígenas de la región central de Nicaragua. Leiden: Research School CNWS, Leiden University (CNWS Publications 112). Capítulo 6 reprinted in Revista de Temas Nicaragüenses 29 (septiembre 2010).
sources.note: No phonology; a full-text search for stress/accent the whole RTN 29 issue for acento/acentu/aguda/tónic/prosod finds nothing in this chapter. Useful only as a pointer to Constenla Umaña 1994 'Las lenguas de la Gran Nicoya', Vínculos 18-19: 191-208 (pp. 194-197 on Matagalpa territory and pseudo-etymologies of toponyms). PDF downloaded to the work dir, a full-text search for stress/accent and deleted (not kept).

sources.citation: Salamanca, Danilo. 1994. "Lenguas extintas en el Pacífico nicaragüense." Wani (Revista del Caribe Nicaragüense) 15: 38-46.
sources.note: Matagalpa is explicitly excluded from the discussion (p. 39: 'Estoy excluyendo de la discusión el matagalpa, o los dialectos del sumo.. ya que éstos pueden ser afiliados a la familia misumalpa'); article treats only Chorotega-Mangue, Nahuat/Nicarao, Subtiava genealogically; nothing on accent. PDF image-only; pp. 38-40 read from page renders.

sources.citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo. 1987. "Elementos de fonología comparada de las lenguas misumalpas." Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 13(1): 129-161. DOI 10.15517/rfl.v13i1.21061
sources.note: Nothing on Matagalpa stress. p.132 sec.0(e): the sources generally do not transcribe suprasegmental features adequately, so reconstruction is limited to vowels and consonants; sec.7: all Matagalpa sources are brief vocabularies reproduced in Lehmann 1920:599-604, ~150 lexical items in total; sec.1.1 (p.133) gives only a segmental inventory for Matagalpa (m n p k b d h r w [j]; vowels i a u) with orthographic observations.
sources.venue: Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 13

sources.citation: Campbell, Lyle. 1975. "Cacaopera." Anthropological Linguistics 17: 146-153.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: First-hand rememberer data on Cacaopera (sister language, caca1244) with phonetic transcription; may comment on stress. Not Matagalpa proper.

sources.citation: Valle, Alfonso. 1944. Interpretación de nombres geográficos indígenas de Nicaragua. Managua: Talleres Gráficos Pérez. [Reprinted in full in Revista Conservadora (del Pensamiento Centroamericano) no. 56, mayo 1965, 52 pp.]
sources.note: No phonology content. Preface (RC 56 p. 1-2 of the reprint) recounts that Valle obtained a Matagalpa vocabulary directly from Indians of Matagalpa and Jinotega in 1908 (published by Lehmann) and in 1922 sent Lehmann 'un acervo más copioso del matagalpa' for a planned new book that was never published - i.e. a larger unpublished Matagalpa vocabulary may survive in Lehmann's Nachlass (Ibero-Amerikanisches Institut, Berlin). Isolated pronunciation notes concern Nahuatl/Spanish names only (e.g. 'Se pronuncia Nicaraocáli').

sources.citation: Le Conte, René. 1921. "Une nouvelle classification des langues indiennes du Centre-Amérique." Journal de la Société des Américanistes 13(2): 339-340.
sources.note: classification list only (p. 339 scanned read inline on the Persée page; p. 340 not displayed); no phonology: '.. a) Nicaragua Oriental (familles guatuso; miskito-sumo-ulua; matagalpa..'
sources.venue: Journal de la Société des Américanistes

sources.citation: Lehmann, Walter. 1920. Zentral-Amerika, Teil I: Die Sprachen Zentral-Amerikas.., Bd. 2, pp. 599-604 (Matagalpa: vocabularies of Noguera/Berendt, Sapper, Brinton, with Lehmann's notes). Berlin: Dietrich Reimer.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: The complete primary corpus of Matagalpa per Constenla 1987; only place where an incidental remark on Betonung or consistent accent marking (e.g. in Sapper's list) could exist. Public domain; Google Books full view ids 8gc5AQAAMAAJ / Gwg5AQAAMAAJ and HathiTrust copies exist but were blocked to automated access.

sources.citation: Lehmann, Walter. 1910. "Ergebnisse einer Forschungsreise in Mittelamerika und México 1907-1909." Zeitschrift für Ethnologie 42: 687-749 (Misquito-Sumo-Matagalpa section, pp. ca. 714-722).
sources.note: No phonology: classification, former extent of the language from toponyms in -li ('water'), a short comparative word table (Misquito, Tauaxca, Ulua, Matagalpa, Cacaopera) and remarks on possessive prefixes. Nothing on accent (no Betonung/Akzent/betont in the section).

sources.citation: Brinton, Daniel G. 1895 [trad. 2010]. "Familia lingüística Matagalpa de America Central" (traducción de 'The Matagalpan linguistic stock of Central America' por Federico Ramón Mairena Vásquez, con notas del traductor y adendum). Revista de Temas Nicaragüenses 23 (marzo 2010): 136-155.
sources.note: 'Fonética' paragraph (p. 139) = Brinton's: sounds offer little difficulty; Mendoza's words in Spanish alphabet, 'la i y la k debe ser pronunciadas forzosamente'; Noguera's in Berendt's system. Translator's notes *a-*f: absence of 'f' and 'ñ' in the glossary, possessive -ke/-ki, verb conjugation; nothing on accent. downloaded, a full-text search for stress/accent (acent|tilde|aguda|grave|pronunci|fonétic|sílaba), deleted.

sources.citation: Brinton, Daniel G. 1895. "The Matagalpan linguistic stock of Central America." Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 34: 403-415.
sources.note: 'Phonetics' paragraph (pp. 405-406) says only that the sounds offer little difficulty to a Spanish student, Mendoza's (Cacaopera) words are in Spanish orthography ('the i and the k should be pronounced forcibly'), Noguera's (Matagalpa) words in Berendt's system; no statement on accent or stress. Some vocabulary items carry acute accents but no rule is given; the grammatical material is Cacaopera (Mendoza), not Matagalpa proper.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society

sources.citation: Belt, Thomas. 1874. The Naturalist in Nicaragua: A narrative of a residence at the gold mines of Chontales; journeys in the savannahs and forests. London: John Murray. (ch. XVI, pp. 293-294; Spanish transl. by J. Incer, 'El naturalista en Nicaragua', Colección Cultural Banco de América.)
sources.note: Only: 'Places apparently of less consequence in Segovia often end in the termination "lee" strongly accented, as Jamaily, Esterly, Daraily, &c., and in "guina" pronounced "weena"' (p. 294) - final stress on the toponymic ending -lí as heard in 1872; no statement about the language's word stress.

sources.citation: Noguera, Víctor Jesús (coll. 1855); Berendt, C. Hermann (copy, Advertencia and Nota, Masaya 1874). "Vocabulario de la lengua popoluca de Matagalpa." Manuscript, University of Pennsylvania, Kislak Center, Berendt-Brinton Linguistic Collection, Ms. Coll. 700 Item 124. 12 leaves.
sources.note: Berendt's 'Advertencia' (ms pp. III-V = pp. 13-15) gives the area where 'popoluca' was spoken, the Nahuatl etymology of 'popoluca' and 'chontal', and Noguera's biography; the 'Nota' (p. 16) counts lexical resemblances (3 Mexican words, 5 Ulua, 1 Lenca, 1 Moskito..). No orthographic key and no remark on accent; the word list itself is largely unaccented (wordlist-only data).
